title: An Overview of Statistics

confusionCorner.body: Beginners often think statistics is only about calculations. But [[imp:the real power is in the interpretation and decision-making]]. A computer can crunch numbers, but only a human can decide what the numbers actually mean for a business, a health study, or a public policy.
confusionCorner.title: Statistics ≠ Just Numbers

steps: The NRF (National Retail Federation) collects sales data from many stores across the country.
These data are organized and summarized to compute the percent changes.
Analysts interpret the numbers to forecast future trends.
This entire process — from collecting data to making a forecast — is [[kw:statistics]] in action!
examples.prompt: Consider the statement: 'The NRF expects holiday sales to decline 1% versus a 3.4% drop the previous year.' Where does this information come from?
examples.title: Example A — Seeing the Big Picture
Example B — Not Just Numbers

Explain to a partner: What four actions must happen to raw data before a statement like this can be made?
examples.prompt: Explain to a partner why the statement 'EIA projects total U.S. natural gas consumption will decline by 2.6 percent in 2009 and increase by 0.5 percent in 2010' is an example of statistics.
steps: First, the Energy Information Administration had to collect data on natural gas usage.
Then they organized and summarized the figures to get the percentages.
Finally, they interpreted the pattern to make the projection.
All four actions — collect, organize, summarize, interpret — define statistics.
The data consist of the yes/no answers from the 1017 survey respondents.
The decision (or interpretation) is that a high percentage of women get regular check-ups.
This is a descriptive summary, but could also lead to health policy decisions.
examples.prompt: Identify the data and the decision in this statement: 'A survey of 1017 men and women found that 76% of women had a physical exam within the previous year.'
examples.title: Example C — Your Turn

discoveryHook.scenario: Every day we see claims like '70% of women had a physical exam last year' or 'gas prices will rise 2.6%'. These statements come from collecting and analyzing data. Welcome to the world of statistics, where raw numbers become powerful insights that help us make decisions!

questions.feedbackIfWrong: Statistics helps us turn data into informed decisions.
hints: It's what you ultimately do after looking at the data.
The word starts with 'd'.

The Latin word 'status' gives us the modern term for 'statistics'. What did 'status' originally mean?
hints: Think about early government record‑keeping.
It's a four‑letter word.

The four actions are collect, organize, analyze, and interpret. 'Predict' is a possible result, but not an official part of the definition.
hints: The four actions are mentioned in the definition.
Check carefully what appears in the formal definition.

blocks.title: What Is Statistics?

70% of unmarried men alive at 65 vs. 90% of married men

explanation: [[kw:Data]] consist of information coming from observations, counts, measurements, or responses.
[[kw:Statistics]] is the science of collecting, organizing, analyzing, and interpreting data in order to make decisions.
You encounter statistics daily: opinion polls, sports scores, medical study results, and economic forecasts.
The word 'statistics' comes from the Latin [[imp:status]], meaning 'state', because early uses involved government census data.

teacherCues: Show a USA TODAY Snapshot graphic and ask: 'What story does this data tell?'
Write 'Statistics = Data + Decisions' on the board.

questions.prompt: A ___ is the complete collection of all elements (scores, people, measurements) that are of interest in a study.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The complete group is called the population.
hints: It starts with 'p', like 'parameter'.
It's the whole group, not just a part.
The population is the entire group you want to make a conclusion about.
It's not just the 200 you asked.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The population is all students at that college.
questions.prompt: If you survey 200 students at a college to estimate the average number of hours all students at that college study, what is the population? (Answer with one word: 'students')

hints: It was computed from the 900 stations.

questions.prompt: In the gasoline price survey (900 stations), is the $2.75 average a characteristic of the population or the sample?

confusionCorner.title: The Sample Is Not the Population!
confusionCorner.body: A common mistake is to think the sample is the whole story. Remember: the sample only [[imp:estimates]] the population truth. A different sample (say, a different 900 gas stations) could give a slightly different average. The population parameter (true average) does not change.

teacherCues: Draw a large circle labeled 'Population' and a smaller circle inside it labeled 'Sample'. Ask: 'Why don't we just study the whole circle every time?'
Hand out a small bag of M&Ms and ask students to take a sample of 5 candies to describe the color distribution of the whole bag.

steps: The population is the entire group you want to draw a conclusion about: [[kw:all U.S. adults' responses]].
The sample is the actual group that gave you data: [[kw:the 1500 surveyed adults' responses]].
The sample data set consists of 855 'yes' answers and 645 'no' answers.
Notice the sample is a subset of the population.
examples.prompt: A survey asked 1500 U.S. adults if they thought there was solid evidence of global warming; 855 said yes. Identify the population and the sample.
examples.title: Example A — Identifying Population and Sample

steps: The population depends on the actual group you intend to study.
If the survey only sampled California residents, the population would be adults in California.
If the survey only included people with landlines, the population would be U.S. adults with landlines.
Always define the population based on the exact group from which the sample was drawn!
examples.prompt: In the global warming survey, could the population be something other than 'all U.S. adults'? Explain to a partner.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: If the survey only called California landline numbers, what would the population actually be?
examples.title: Example B — Changing the Population

steps: The entire population of interest is all gasoline stations in the U.S.
900 stations are only a subset, so it is a [[kw:sample]].
A census would require checking every station — impractical!
The average price from the sample ($2.75) is used to estimate the true national average.
examples.title: Example C — Census or Sample?
examples.prompt: The U.S. Department of Energy surveys approximately 900 gasoline stations to determine the average price of regular gasoline. Is the 900 a population or a sample?

discoveryHook.scenario: Imagine you want to know the average height of all high school students in the U.S. Measuring all 15 million of them is impossible! Instead, you select a smaller group — a sample — and use their heights to estimate the true average. This is the fundamental idea behind sampling.

legend.meaning: the whole group (e.g., all adults in the U.S.)
a carefully chosen subset (e.g., 1500 surveyed adults)

rows.1: Often too large to measure completely
All registered voters in the U.S.

explanation: A [[kw:population]] is the complete collection of all individuals, objects, or measurements that you are interested in studying.
A [[kw:sample]] is a subset, or part, of the population.
A [[kw:census]] is a study that attempts to collect data from every member of the population. However, due to cost, time, or accessibility, a census is often impractical.
The goal of a sample is to be [[imp:representative]] of the population, so we can draw conclusions about the whole group from just the sample.
When a sample is not representative (biased), any conclusions are unreliable.

blocks.title: Populations and Samples

discoveryHook.scenario: When you hear 'average starting salary of petroleum engineers is $83,121', that number came from a sample of 200 colleges. The true average of all petroleum engineers might be a little different. The number from the sample is a statistic; the true, unknown number for the whole population is a parameter.

examples.prompt: The average SAT score of the 2182 students who accepted admission to Northwestern University in 2009 is 1442. Is this number a parameter or a statistic?
examples.title: Example A — Parameter or Statistic?
steps: Identify the group: the 2182 students are the entire group of accepted students. That's the population (for this university).
Because the number describes an entire population, it is a [[kw:parameter]].
If the study had only looked at a sample of those students, the average would be a statistic.
Key: If you have data for the whole group of interest, you've got a parameter.

examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: If the survey had contacted all college career centers in the U.S., would that change your answer?
examples.prompt: A survey of 200 college career centers reported an average starting salary of $83,121. Is this a parameter or a statistic?
steps: The 200 centers are a sample, not the entire population of all career centers.
Therefore the average $83,121 is a [[kw:statistic]].
Even though the number looks precise, it's an estimate of the true (population) average.
Only a census of all career centers would give a parameter.
examples.title: Example B — The Survey Trap

steps: The number comes from all 30 MLB teams — the entire league of interest.
Because it covers the whole population, it is a [[kw:parameter]].
Note: If you later take a sample of 10 teams and compute their average salary, that average would be a statistic.
examples.prompt: In 2009, Major League Baseball teams spent a total of $2,655,395,194 on players' salaries. Does this total describe a parameter or a statistic?
examples.title: Example C — Census Parameter

blocks.title: Parameter and Statistic

legend.meaning: true value for the whole population

rows.2: Statistic (known, varies from sample to sample)

explanation: A [[kw:parameter]] is a numerical measurement describing some characteristic of a population.
A [[kw:statistic]] is a numerical measurement describing some characteristic of a sample.
Because a population parameter is usually unknown, we use sample statistics to [[imp:estimate]] them.
Mnemonic: [[imp:P]]arameter goes with [[imp:P]]opulation; [[imp:S]]tatistic goes with [[imp:S]]ample.
A sample statistic can vary from sample to sample, but the population parameter is fixed (though unknown).

questions.prompt: A report states: '52% of the 50 U.S. governors are Democrats.' Is 52% a parameter or a statistic?
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Because all 50 governors are included (the entire population of U.S. governors), the 52% is a population parameter.
hints: Think about whether the data include the whole group of interest.
All 50 governors are counted, not just a sample.

questions.prompt: A sample statistic is used to ___ a population parameter.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: A sample statistic provides an estimate of the true population parameter.
hints: We can't always measure the whole population, so we use the sample to make a good guess.
This word starts with 'e'.

questions.feedbackIfWrong: The sample statistic varies from sample to sample; the population parameter remains constant.
hints: Parameters are fixed for a given population.
The measure from the sample is what varies.
questions.prompt: Which one changes if you take a different sample — the parameter or the statistic? (Answer with one word)

confusionCorner.title: Fixed vs. Variable
confusionCorner.body: A population parameter (like the true mean height of all U.S. adults) does not change — it's a single, fixed number, even if we don't know it. A sample statistic (like the mean height of 500 people) will vary from one sample to the next. [[imp:Parameters are constant; statistics vary.]]

teacherCues: Write on the board: 'Parameter → Population, Statistic → Sample'. Underline the 'p' and 's' matches.
Ask: 'What letter does Parameter share with Population? What letter does Statistic share with Sample?'

questions.prompt: Which branch of statistics involves creating charts and calculating averages from a data set? (Answer with one word: descriptive or inferential)
hints: This branch just summarizes what you see.
It's the 'what' of the data, not the 'so what'.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: Organizing, summarizing, and displaying data is descriptive statistics.
Inferential statistics uses sample data to draw conclusions about a population.
hints: This branch deals with inference — going beyond the data.
It starts with 'i'.
questions.prompt: Using a sample to make a conclusion about a population is called ___ statistics.

questions.feedbackIfWrong: This statement is an inference drawn from the descriptive results (70% vs. 90%).
hints: This statement goes beyond the raw percentages.
It suggests a relationship for the broader population.
questions.prompt: In the married‑men study, is the statement 'Being married is associated with a longer life for men' descriptive or inferential?

examples.title: Example A — Spotting the Branches
steps: Descriptive part: '44% of the analysts in the sample were wrong.' This summarizes the data.
Inferential jump: 'This suggests that forecasting tech earnings is extremely difficult, even for experts.'
The inference goes beyond the sample to make a statement about the broader world of financial forecasting.
Remember: descriptive = what you found; inferential = what it might mean.
examples.prompt: A study found that in a sample of Wall Street analysts, 44% incorrectly forecasted high‑tech earnings. Identify the descriptive statistic and propose a possible inference.

steps: The descriptive statistics are the two percentages (76% and 60%) obtained from the sample.
An inference might be: 'Women tend to get regular check‑ups more often than men.'
However, the inference applies only to the population from which the sample was drawn, not every single human.
Inferential statements always carry some uncertainty because they are based on a sample.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: Why can't you say for certain that all women are more likely to get check‑ups?
examples.prompt: A survey of 1017 adults found that 76% of women and 60% of men had a physical exam in the previous year. Explain to a partner which part is descriptive and what inference you could make.
examples.title: Example B — From Data to Decision

steps: The statement that the census overcounted by 1.3 million is [[kw:descriptive]] — it summarizes the result of a post‑census evaluation.
An inference could be: 'Census methods need improvement to avoid overcounting in the future.'
Or: 'Funding allocations based on census data might be slightly inaccurate.'
In each case, you're moving from the number itself to a broader conclusion.
examples.prompt: The Census Bureau reports that the 2000 census overcounted the U.S. population by 1.3 million people. Is this statement descriptive or inferential? What inference might you draw?
examples.title: Example C — Your Own Inference

teacherCues: Hold up a class's test score list: 'If I just calculate the average and show a histogram, that's descriptive. If I say the class average suggests that the teaching method worked better than last year's method, that's inferential.'
Show a graph (bar chart) of the marital status survival rates and ask: 'Which part is descriptive? What inference could you make?'

discoveryHook.scenario: You read: 'A study of men aged 48 found that 70% of unmarried men were alive at age 65, while 90% of married men were alive at 65.' The percentages are descriptive — they just summarize the data. But concluding that marriage might contribute to longer life is an inference — it goes beyond the raw numbers.

confusionCorner.title: Don't Overclaim!
confusionCorner.body: Inferential statistics does not prove something with 100% certainty. It only provides evidence supporting a conclusion. Always use words like [[imp:'suggests', 'indicates', or 'is associated with']] instead of 'proves'. For instance, the married‑men study does not prove marriage causes longer life — it only shows an association.

blocks.title: Descriptive and Inferential Statistics

legend.meaning: the 'so what' — extending to the population

explanation: [[kw:Descriptive statistics]] involves the organization, summarization, and display of data. This includes graphs, averages, and tables.
[[kw:Inferential statistics]] involves using a sample to draw conclusions (make inferences) about a population. It relies on probability.
Descriptive statistics says what the data show; inferential statistics says what the data [[imp:mean for the larger world]].
Example: '44% of analysts incorrectly forecasted earnings' is descriptive. 'Therefore, even professionals find the market hard to predict' is an inference.
Virtually every medical study, political poll, and business forecast uses both branches.

rows.2: The true average height of all students at this school is between 5'5" and 5'7" with 95% confidence

discoveryHook.scenario: You're reading an article about a new diet that 'helped 80% of participants lose weight'. Should you trust it? By applying a simple blueprint — Understand, Solve, Conclude — you can dissect any statistical claim and decide if the evidence is solid.

examples.title: Example A — Blueprint in Action
examples.prompt: Apply the blueprint to: 'A survey of 1000 U.S. adults found that 59% think buying a home is the best investment.' (Source: Rasmussen Reports)
steps: Understand: The study asked 1000 U.S. adults about their investment opinion.
Solve: The 1000 adults are a sample (subset) of all U.S. adults, so the 59% is a statistic. The statement just reports the percentage, so it is descriptive.

Conclude: The study provides a descriptive statistic (59% of this sample). No inference is explicitly made by the study itself, but you could infer that a majority of all U.S. adults might feel this way, keeping in mind the sample may be biased.
Understand: The population is the top 100 companies. The magazine received data from 85 companies.

Solve: Because only 85 out of 100 responded, the data represent a sample. Any statistics (like average employee satisfaction) from the 85 would be sample statistics. The analysis would be descriptive of those 85, but any generalization to all 100 would be inferential.
Conclude: The 85 is a sample, so any number is a statistic. Since only 85% responded, the sample may be biased (non‑response bias) — those who responded might be happier than those who didn't.
examples.peerPrompt:
Without looking back...

Explain to a partner: Is the group of 85 a population or a sample? Does it matter that only 85 responded?
examples.prompt: A magazine sends questionnaires to all companies in Fortune's top 100 best companies to work for and receives responses from 85 of them. Identify the components using the blueprint.
examples.title: Example B — Peer Blueprint

examples.prompt: A quality control inspector selects 20 light bulbs from the day's production and tests them; all 20 work perfectly. The inspector concludes that all bulbs produced that day are perfect. Use the blueprint to evaluate this conclusion.
steps: Understand: The population is the entire day's production of light bulbs. The sample is the 20 selected bulbs.
Solve: The 20 bulbs are a sample, so the 100% defect‑free rate is a statistic. The inspector's conclusion that all bulbs are perfect is an inference about the population.

Conclude: The inference may be too strong because the sample is very small. With only 20 bulbs, there could still be defective bulbs in the untested batch. A larger sample would be needed for a reliable inference.
examples.title: Example C — Spot the Flaw

confusionCorner.body: The size of the sample affects how trustworthy an inference is. A larger, representative sample gives a more reliable picture of the population. [[imp:Be skeptical of inferences drawn from tiny or voluntary samples.]]
confusionCorner.title: Sample Size Matters

hints: It's the third step.
It rhymes with 'include'.
questions.prompt: What final blueprint step involves deciding if the inference is reasonable? (Answer with one word)
questions.feedbackIfWrong: The final step is Conclude, where you evaluate the quality of the inference.

explanation: A systematic way to analyze any statistical study uses three steps: [[imp:Understand → Solve → Conclude]].
Step 1 – [[kw:Understand]]: Identify the context. Who or what is being studied? What data were collected? What is the population of interest?
Step 2 – [[kw:Solve]]: Classify the components. Is the group a population or a sample? Are reported numbers parameters or statistics? Is the analysis descriptive or inferential?
Step 3 – [[kw:Conclude]]: State your classifications clearly. If an inference is made, note whether it seems reasonable based on the sample.

legend.meaning: judge the quality of the evidence

rows.2: What is the group? What data are given?
Population or sample? Parameter or statistic? Descriptive or inferential?
Is the inference reasonable? Are there any biases?

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid: Analyzing a Statistical Study
teacherCues: Project a short news article with statistics. Ask students to underline the data and circle the conclusions.
Emphasize: 'Blueprint steps work for any study — just Identify, Classify, Conclude.'

presenterNotes: In Block 1, emphasize that statistics is more than just crunching numbers — it's a decision‑making science. Use the USA TODAY Snapshot as a visual hook.
For Block 2, the M&M sampling activity is a great hands‑on way to illustrate sample vs. population.
Block 3's mnemonic device (P‑P, S‑S) should be repeated until students automatically connect parameter with population.
When covering Block 4, stress the difference between just reporting data (descriptive) and making a claim beyond the data (inferential). Use the phrase 'descriptive = what; inferential = so what?'
The Blueprint Aid (Block 5) can be applied to any statistical claim students encounter in the news. Encourage them to use the Understand‑Solve‑Conclude framework outside of class.
